newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine peso starts stronger than expected.
newsitem.headline: Philippine peso starts stronger than expected.

text.p: The Philippine peso opened stronger than expected on Monday after last week's de facto devaluation while the share market stormed higher, traders said.
The peso was trading at around 28 per dollar in early trade compared to last Friday when it hit a near four-year low of 29.45, a plunge of 11.5 percent on the day.
Last week, the central bank, fast running out of dollars to defend the peso, surrendered to speculators and allowed its currency to float in a wider band.
Central bank governor Gabriel Singson told Reuters on Sunday night that the bank would still intervene to calm down the market.
In the first hour of trading only a tiny $5.5 million dollars had been traded, a fraction of the normal level.
Traders had said before the market opened that they expected the currency to move closer to 30 pesos to the dollar.
The Philippine stock market responded by surging as it did on Friday immediately after the the peso was freed up. The main index opened on Monday just over one percent higher at 2,730.52.
Investors went on a shopping spree as the peso slump has made stocks cheaper for foreigners and on hopes that the weaker currency would boost some local companies, particularly exporters.

Traders said they hope the central bank will now feel free to relax one of the key measures it used to defend the peso against speculators last week -- high interest rates which were starting to bite into economic growth.
The plight of the Philippine peso follows the de facto devaluation of the Thai baht two weeks ago which triggered speculative attacks against Southeast Asian currencies.
Economists said the Philippine currency's fall was certain to lead to higher inflation and would reduce economic growth this year.
But government officials claimed the impact would be slight though President Fidel Ramos at the weekend urged Filipinos to stay calm.

The International Monetary Fund (IMF) immediately pledged to support Manila in what is the IMF's first chance to try out emergency funding rules introduced after the Mexico financial crisis that erupted at the end of 1994.

An IMF source in Washington told Reuters that accelerated procedures to offer the Philippines a support package of at least $600 million relied on rules under the IMF's so-called emergency financing mechanism.
